bmo_core_1809151.summary: The case tests whether an agent can drive an enterprise Kerberos-proxy iframe-auth regression from report → mozregression range → private HTTP log → distinguishing a proxy-generated X-Frame-Options: deny from an origin policy → backing out Firefox bug 1629307, with reporter verification in Nightly. The graph is broadly faithful to the thread: the clarification chain mirrors comments 1–11, the measurement-class edges (mozregression, HTTP log, Nightly test) are correctly clarification_only, and the root cause in satisfaction_conditions matches participant3's comment 9 analysis. Two structural problems would corrupt scoring: one hard required_info id is ungettable (it exists only as engineer log-reading), and the canonical chain asks the user to verify a Nightly containing the backout BEFORE any edge proposes the backout, inverting the thread's actual order and making the historically correct move (propose backout at N3) off-path. Release-uplift bookkeeping is also baked into the full-match requirements.
bmo_core_1809151.strengths: Measurement-class handling is correct throughout: mozregression (e1), the HTTP log capture (e2), the proxy-side XFO-disable probe (e3), and the Nightly test (e4) are all clarification_only, and none of their results is pre-loaded into N0's volunteered_info — the agent must ask. The Task body is a clean opening report (proxy Kerberos policy, 108.0.1 regression, iframe-only failure, proxy logs show no auth, multiple machines, beta/Nightly affected, proxy unchanged) with zero later-thread knowledge — no mention of bug 1629307, X-Frame-Options, or the backout. The root cause in satisfaction_condition #1 matches participant3's comment 9 analysis precisely (1629307 disabled auth prompts for responses that XFO/CSP would block, and the XFO here was the proxy's unauthenticated fallback). Satisfaction_condition #3 correctly forbids settling on "disable X-Frame-Options / reconfigure the proxy", which is exactly the brush-off the reporter rejected with evidence in comment 11 ("I found no option to disable any X-Frame-Options. We do not manipulate any content of the website"). The engineer-only items (engineers_trace_regression_to_bug_1629307, bug_1629307_suppresses_auth_for_iframe_responses_blocked_by_xfo, proxy_xfo_response_causes_kerberos_authentication_to_be_suppressed) are properly parked in info_inferred_by_engineer. persona_hint matches a cooperative enterprise IT reporter who ran mozregression, mailed a sensitive log, and tested Nightly. The single opening attachment 9311319 (FF_issue.png) is hooked as opening_images and the file exists; the counterfactual candidates on e1/e3/e4 are well-chosen and correctly flag whether the solution should change.

gh_curl_curl_10936.summary: The case tests a long, cold-trail HTTP/2 use-after-free hunt: two maintainer 'just upgrade' resolutions that field testing falsified, then a lifecycle trace showing nghttp2 closing a stream long after the easy handle was freed, then a patch trial that confirmed clearing the nghttp2 stream user data before RST_STREAM. The graph's skeleton is faithful — both blind paths are real, the patch trials are correctly modeled as clarifications, and the multi-user merge is declared. The main defect is that one clarification answer on e4 puts the maintainer's key insight ('the stream's user-data pointer is not cleared first') into the user's mouth, leaking the fix that the terminal solution is supposed to require the agent to derive; a second answer on e2 gives the reporter reproducibility he explicitly denied having at that point in the thread. A release-version gate in required_elements and a diagnosis-flavored terminal symptom are lesser issues.
gh_curl_curl_10936.strengths: Both blind paths are genuinely falsified in the thread and are labeled correctly: e1 ('test 8.2.1 / current git, it is probably already fixed') matches c5/c13 and was refuted by c15 ('Still see this with cURL 8.2.1 and nghttp2 1.55.1, reverting cURL to 7.86.0 works around the issue'); e3 ('related to #12356, fixed in 8.5.0', c23) was refuted twice, by c26 ('No, the issue still exists') and c28 (reporter's 8.5.0 + nghttp2 1.58.0 backtrace). Measurement-class handling is exactly right: the maintainer-requested set_stream_user_data(NULL) patch trial (c39 → c45, 16 h vs the usual 6-7 crashes) and the reporter's two-day PR #12562 run (c47) are modeled as clarification edges with the measured result as the user answer, not as solution edges. The multi-user merge (reporter + participant5's crash-dump statistics + participant6's trace analysis) is explicitly declared in the e2, e4 and e5 comments. Gettability is sound — every id in e6.required_info is granted by an earlier clarification or a volunteered node id, and the root-cause id is correctly kept in info_inferred_by_engineer. The Task body is clean of later knowledge, the crash-dump details (discarded data_s, 317/318 NGHTTP2_STREAM_CLOSED with one NGHTTP2_REFUSED_STREAM) match c18 verbatim, and the stated root cause, the falsified-move prohibition and the verification requirement in satisfaction_conditions all match how the thread actually ended.

confirmed_findings.verifier_reasoning: Thread check confirms the attribution. The user-side deep analysis is c37 (participant6): http2_data_done -> nghttp2_submit_rst_stream -> item marked cancelled -> '15 minutes later' nghttp2 gets the cancelled outbound item, does NOT skip it, opens the stream, then must close it and calls on_stream_close on the easy handle 'closed 15 minutes ago'; c37 ends 'I currently feel it's nghttp2's problem for trying to open and close stream for a cancelled item.' The word 'user data' never appears on the user side there; c35 is the closest and blames ob_syn cleanup inside nghttp2, not user data. The user-data insight is maintainer participant3's: c36 ('PR 12562 with some small changes in clearing stream user data and checks on the seen user data in on_stream_close') and c39 ('you could check ... nghttp2_session_set_stream_user_data(ctx->h2, stream->id, NULL); at the beginning of http2_data_done() before nghttp2_submit_rst_stream()'). c45 confirms the direction of learning: participant6 asks afterwards 'So the real story is the nghttp2 requires the user to take care of the user data before cancelling, right?'. So the e4 answer puts the maintainer's hypothesis in the user's mouth, and its content is verbatim required_elements_for_full_match[2] ('clears_stream_user_data_before_rst_stream') plus half the root cause, obtainable from a fairly generic question pattern ('What does http2_data_done do for the timed-out stream?'). Two mitigations keep this at medium rather than high: (a) the same hypothesis is legitimately encoded one edge later at e5 as a handler-requested measurement (c39 -> c45), so the graph is duplicating rather than inventing it; (b) whether curl clears the pointer is a static, code-inspectable fact a source-reading user could report if asked, which is inside the measurement-class allowance. Correct fix is the reviewer's: keep the thread-supported c37 mechanics in the answer and move 'user-data pointer not cleared' into e6.info_inferred_by_engineer / inference_hint.

gh_curl_curl_11203.summary: The case tests whether an agent can drive a Hyper-backend HTTP/2 slowness report from "three URLs take a minute" to the real defect — curl's Hyper integration creating a hyper_clientconn per request, re-sending the HTTP/2 connection preface and provoking GOAWAY-driven 30-second retries — and then to the accepted temporary mitigation of disabling HTTP/2 for Hyper. The graph is substantially faithful: the diagnostic chain, the one blind path (PR 11344), the root cause, and the measurement-class modelling all match the thread. The defects are concentrated in the last two steps, where the graph inverts the thread's proposal→verification order and puts the mitigation itself into the reporter's spoken symptoms at N5 and N_terminal, handing the agent part of the answer key. A secondary problem is that satisfaction_conditions requires grounding in "no replacement connection in the trace" (c17), which the accepted GOAWAY-retry mechanism (c23/c35) contradicts.
gh_curl_curl_11203.strengths: The single blind path is correctly identified and correctly labelled: e2's PR 11344 was genuinely falsified for the reporter (c7 participant2 "I made some small changes that resolve the slowness for me. Pr in #11344." followed by c8 participant1 "Does not fix it for @reporter apparently"), and the aftermath node N2_x plus its forward edge match the reporter's own c11 re-measurement (0:01:01,321, plus "the response of first URL got dropped in some cases!"). The root cause in satisfaction_conditions[0] is exactly what the thread established in c23 and c35 (a hyper_clientconn created per request, so the HTTP/2 connection preface + settings are re-sent before every request, which servers answer with GOAWAY, producing the 30-second retries and dropped requests), and the accepted mitigation matches c41/c42 (disable HTTP/2 for the Hyper backend, PR 12191) including the c40/c45 note that a real fix needs a connection-filter rearchitecture. Measurement-class handling is unusually disciplined: the double executor poll (c2), the --http1.1 comparison (c23), the Wireshark capture (c23) and the master rebuild (c44/c46) are all clarification edges, not solutions. Engineer-side inference (root cause, GOAWAY behaviour, the disable-HTTP/2 proposal) is properly quarantined in info_inferred_by_engineer rather than hard required_info, and every required_info id is gettable. The multi-user merge is explicitly declared on e1 and e3, the opening body is free of any later diagnosis, and the persona hint matches the reporter's behaviour precisely (c3: "I'm clueless about such internal details", alongside his own debug builds, DEBUGF instrumentation and timing scripts).

Keep the 'HTTP/2 disabled' attribution only in e6's info_inferred_by_engineer / solution text.

refuted_claims.claim: The verification measurement is placed BEFORE the solution edge that proposes the mitigation, and its question patterns name the fix, so obtaining e6's mandatory L3 evidence requires the fix to already have been disclosed.
refuted_claims.why_refuted: REFUTED as a distinct defect. The contract's MEASUREMENT-CLASS RULE explicitly covers this shape: handler-initiated try-builds and config-toggle probes are clarification edges 'even when the probed toggle doubles as a workaround', so probe (e5) -> verified state (N5) -> formal mitigation (e6) is the sanctioned encoding, and it is what satisfaction_conditions[4] ('reporter verification ... before declaring the slowness resolved') requires. question_patterns are agent-side matching templates, not user utterances — nothing in them is spoken by the simulator (only symptoms_visible and user_answer_in_this_oncall are), so naming 'the Hyper HTTP/2 disablement' or 'PR 12191' in a pattern leaks nothing; matching is token-overlap so an agent that never says '12191' still matches. An agent can derive the probe itself from N3 (--http1.1 finishes in 300 ms vs >60 s) and N4 (a fresh preface per request), which is exactly how participant7 got there in c41. The real user-side reveal at this position is the N5 wording, already captured by finding 1; the edge ordering itself is not a defect.

refuted_claims.claim: satisfaction_conditions[1] requires grounding in "no replacement connection appears in the trace", which contradicts the root cause the same key demands (GOAWAY -> delayed retry / dropped request), so a correct agent can be scored against a contradicting grounding item.
refuted_claims.why_refuted: REFUTED. The quotes are accurate but they describe different time windows and do not actually contradict. c17 (participant1) is about what happens DURING the ~30 s pause — the pause is not an SSL timeout followed by a silent reconnect, 'the trace shows no new connection ... a curl will not silently do a new connection if a transfer fails in the middle'. c23/c35 describe what happens at the END of the pause — the server sends GOAWAY and curl+hyper then sets up a new connection and retries. Both are genuine collected evidence in the thread, and sc[0] is deliberately hedged ('can provoke server GOAWAY behavior, delayed retries, or dropped requests'). sc[0] also states exactly c35's mechanism, so the 'wrong_root_cause' class is misapplied. Residual nit only: sc[1]'s bare phrasing could be tightened to 'no replacement connection is opened during the pause itself' to remove any chance of a judge reading a conflict; that is optional polish, not a required fix.

gh_etcd-io_etcd_20418.summary: The case is a long Antithesis-driven investigation of a linearizability violation in etcd: a stale ReadIndex is returned after a leader stall, ultimately traced to etcd's linearizableReadLoop reusing the same ReadIndex request ID (RequestCtx) across retries, interacting badly with raft's readOnly map/queue. The graph is substantially faithful on the load-bearing points: the single blind path (e3, the select/leadership-race guess) is genuinely falsified in the thread (c19 "First blind guess", c23 "celebration was too early... the last one got a reproduction on branch with the fix", c26 "it was early bad guess"); the root cause and the merged mitigation (PR #21399, fresh request ID per retry) match c31/c35/c48; the fix-validation runs are correctly modeled as clarification (measurement) edges rather than solutions. Remaining issues are fidelity-level: a release/backport element baked into required_elements_for_full_match, a missing alternative explanation for the headline rev-3-vs-155 symptom that the thread actually established, a small ordering leak in e5, and one loosely-matched image.
gh_etcd-io_etcd_20418.strengths: The dominant failure mode is avoided: the one blind edge (e3, "leadership/select race") is exactly the attempt the thread falsified, and the aftermath node N3_x quotes the right evidence ("One of three Antithesis runs on the branch containing the initial fix reproduced the same failure", c23) with the right image (img3 = the c23 screenshot). The e3 comment correctly cites both the retraction (c23) and the reporter's later self-assessment (c26 "it was early bad guess"). Measurement-class handling is right throughout: the instrumentation requests (e2, e4) and the fix-validation runs (e5) are clarification edges with results in user_answer, not solutions, matching c16 (participant1 asking for specific log lines), c19/c31 (instrumentation commits) and c32 (0/4 runs). The root cause in satisfaction_conditions[0] correctly merges participant1's cached-commitIndex mechanism (c35) with participant4's readOnly-queue-advance mechanism (c36/c43), and the graph correctly frames PR #21399 as a verified mitigation rather than a raft-level cure, which is what c47 concluded. satisfaction_conditions[3] and [4] explicitly forbid settling on DB/WAL corruption, the highlighted kvstore.go line, or the select-race fix, and demand repeated fault-test verification before declaring resolution — a direct encoding of the thread's own false-positive lesson (c20 "We need multiple runs and at least 48h of simulation to confirm fix"). Every clarification answer I checked is traceable: rev3/155 (c0), no DB/WAL issue except the missing tombstone (c0), the kvstore.go statistical-debug hit with the instrumented-line-number caveat (c4/c5), the 23.731/24.193 460ms timeline (c11/c15), log-order trust (c17/c24), fault semantics (c18/c24), reused request ID 3744633826720154659 with the readOnly queue state (c31), and 0/4 + periodic + CI results (c32/c49/c55). Its three clauses are all observations: "Docker 28 still cannot route container traffic to Tailscale" (the user's own complaint), "the iptables counters increase along the affected forwarding path" (literally what the c13/c14/c16 `iptables -nvL` dumps show — populated pkts columns on the FORWARD/DOCKER/ts-forward jumps), and "the installation has Tailscale stateful filtering enabled", which is verbatim user-reported state, not engineer inference: c36 (participant2) "on my node stateful-filtering was enabled" and c34 "this Parameter is default since Tailscale 1.66 ... gh_nodejs_node_59364.summary: The case tests whether an agent can move from a vague "Node 22.18 broke our CI, --no-experimental-strip-types fixes it" report to the reporter-specific cause (Mocha 10's module-loading fallback under newly-default type stripping) and the verified fix (upgrade Mocha), without settling for the opt-out flag or for reverting the suspected Node PR. The graph is largely faithful: the opening body, the __dirname/no-`type`-field/Node-24 clarifications, the Mocha 10 discovery, the folded minimal repro, the falsified PR-58657 revert, and the reporter's own confirmation that upgrading Mocha removes the need for the flag all map to real comments (c3, c9, c11–c12, c15, c19, c30). Two fidelity issues remain: the aftermath node N2_x is a dead end with no way back to the canonical path, and satisfaction condition 1 hard-asserts the ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX/error-code mechanism as the *reporter's* root cause even though the thread's own expert warned that repro was "probably significantly different" from what the reporter was seeing.
gh_nodejs_node_59364.strengths: The Task body is a clean reformulation of the opening report with zero downstream knowledge (version boundary, three platforms, the opt-out flag, the LTS-policy complaint) and no diagnosis. Every clarification answer is traceable to a real reporter comment: __dirname undefined and the missing `type` field (c3), Node 24.5.0 also affected and cured by the same flag (c9), Mocha 10 in the project (c19), the Mocha 10 + `mocha --require ts-node/register` minimal repro plus the tsx-not-affected observation (c4, c11, c12), and the verified upgrade (c19). The multi-user fold of participant4's repro is explicitly declared in the e2 comment, and the engineer-side analysis from c15 is correctly parked in info_inferred_by_engineer with the e2 comment explaining it. The Mocha-upgrade probe in e4 is correctly modeled as clarification_only per the measurement-class rule even though the upgrade doubles as the fix, with the actual adoption carrying the S1->S2 transition on e5. The blind path is genuine, not fabricated (c30). Scoping to the reporter's verified resolution while explicitly excluding the still-unresolved tsx/swc/ts-node/Jest/node:test branches (satisfaction condition 4, e5 comment) is exactly right for a thread that was ultimately closed as stale with those sub-issues open. persona_hint matches the reporter's own words in c9 ("one gigantius project, that is 7 years old").

confirmed_findings.location: graph.nodes.N2_x (no outgoing edges; only inbound e3_N2__N2_x)

confirmed_findings.thread_evidence: c30 (participant6): "Tried reverting https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/58657 and the issue persists. I think the issue falls on the fact that we added the 'module-typescript' and 'commonjs-typescript' format to loaders." — the thread moves forward after the failed revert; and the reporter's own resolution (c19, "Upgrading to latest mocha does fix the initial problem") remained available. 10 of the 12 sibling graphs in data/github_v0/graphs wire their *_x aftermath nodes forward (e.g. gh_moby_moby_49498 N2_x -> e3_N2_x__N3).
confirmed_findings.suggested_fix: Add a recovery edge N2_x -> N3 carrying the same clarification as e4 ("upgrade from Mocha 10 to the latest Mocha and rerun without the flag"), so the falsified revert costs a turn but does not make the case unwinnable.
confirmed_findings.verifier_reasoning: Confirmed independently, and the framework code makes it worse than the reviewer argued. (a) Graph fact: N2_x is the target of e3_N2__N2_x and appears in no edge's `from`. (b) Runtime fact: I checked whether the framework repairs absorbing decoys automatically. src/graph_bench/oncall_graph/rollbacks.py exists precisely for this ("decoy destinations absorbing: an agent that matched one blind solution could never leave, and the stall insurance ... terminated the session as failed_dead_end"), but `expand_graph_with_rollbacks` / `autogen_rollback_edges` have ZERO call sites outside their own module — user_simulator/loader.py:45 applies only `expand_graph_with_shortcuts`. So no rollback N2_x->N2 is synthesized at load time. (c) responder.py `_fire_insurance` then hits exactly the documented failure: `edge = self.canonical.get(node_before); if edge is None: # Dead-end node (e.g. N3_x): no canonical path -> fail; self.session.termination_reason = 'failed_dead_end'`. Landing on N2_x therefore kills the session rather than costing a turn. (d) Data-level convention supports it: of the 13 sibling graphs with *_x nodes, 11 wire the aftermath forward (gh_moby_moby_49498 N2_x->e3_N2_x__N3, gh_flutter_flutter_140504 N4_x->N4, etc.); only this graph and gh_expo_expo_24172 leave one absorbing. (e) The trigger is realistic: reverting PR 58657 is a move a Node-triage agent would plausibly make (a core maintainer literally made it, c30). The reviewer's proposed N2_x->N3 recovery edge works; a rollback N2_x->N2 (framework-canonical, restores access to both e3-avoidance and e4) is the cleaner fix. Medium, not high, because the harm is conditional on the agent actually taking the decoy.

confirmed_findings.claim: The graph states the ERR_UNKNOWN_FILE_EXTENSION -> ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX / missed-retry mechanism as "the reporter-specific root cause", but the thread established that mechanism only for another participant's repro and explicitly cautioned that the reporter's case is probably different; the reporter's observed failure (`__dirname` undefined) is consistent with type stripping making import() of the .ts file *succeed* as ESM so Mocha 10 never fell back to require(), not with an unhandled error code.
confirmed_findings.thread_evidence: c15 (participant8) derives the ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX analysis explicitly from "the repro of @participant4" ("because it's using the `import readFile = promises.readFile` syntax"); c16 (same author): "I think the repro from @participant4 is probably significantly different from what @participant3 or @reporter are seeing." The reporter's only stated symptom is c3: "What I saw was that suddenly `__dirname` was not defined." The only reporter-verified fact is c19: "I found that we also use mocha 10 ... Upgrading to latest mocha does fix the initial problem."
confirmed_findings.suggested_fix: Soften condition 1 to require the Mocha-10-loader-order cause (Mocha 10 import()s the .ts file first; under type stripping that path is now taken instead of falling back to require(), so the registered TypeScript hook never runs and the file executes as ESM — hence no `__dirname`), and mark the specific error-code detail as the mechanism established on the folded minimal repro rather than as a mandatory required element.
confirmed_findings.verifier_reasoning: Confirmed, and the reviewer's quotes are accurate. c15 (participant8) scopes the error-code analysis to participant4's repro ("the repro of @participant4 comes down to this ... because it's using the `import readFile = promises.readFile` syntax"), and c16 by the same author says "I think the repro from @participant4 is probably significantly different from what @participant3 or @reporter are seeing." The reporter's only stated symptom is c3 (`__dirname` was not defined) and their only verified fact is c19 (also on Mocha 10; upgrading fixes it, flag no longer needed). Mechanically the two branches diverge from the same root: Mocha 10's esm-utils import()s first and falls back to require() only on ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND / ERR_UNKNOWN_FILE_EXTENSION / ERR_UNSUPPORTED_DIR_IMPORT. If the .ts file contains type-stripping-unsupported syntax you get the new ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX and the retry is missed (participant4's case); if the file strips cleanly, import() now SUCCEEDS and the file runs as ESM, so the ts-node hook never runs and `__dirname` is undefined (the reporter's symptom) — no error code involved at all. The shared, reporter-verified cause is the load-order one (Mocha 10 imports first; Mocha 11 tries require() first so the hook applies). The graph hard-codes the narrower branch: satisfaction_conditions[0] names ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX as "the reporter-specific root cause", and e5's required_elements_for_full_match includes "explains_changed_typescript_error_and_fallback_behavior". A correct answer giving the load-order/ESM-success mechanism would be marked down. Mitigating: participant8 himself generalized ("this can be generalized to any TypeScript syntax not supported by type stripping") and c24 (participant6) applies the error-code theory broadly, so the graph is not fabricating — it is over-specifying a folded-repro mechanism into a mandatory element. Medium.

refuted_claims.claim: The revert of PR 58657 was built and tested by a Node core maintainer against the tsx reproduction, not by the reporter against their Mocha 10 project, yet its outcome is placed on the user side as an observed symptom in the reporter's state.
refuted_claims.why_refuted: The factual premise checks out (c30 is participant6, a Node maintainer, on Aug 11, in the middle of the tsx investigation of c26; the reporter's own resolution was already confirmed Aug 7 in c19, and the reporter never built Node), but it is not a defect under the contract. Every solution edge's aftermath must be reported by the single folded user side — that is structurally forced by the node/edge model, and the contract explicitly says a falsified attempt "lands on an aftermath node (usually named *_x) whose symptoms_visible describe the post-attempt state." The authored text is already outcome-phrased and agent-neutral — "The failure remains after testing a revert of the suspected `.js` handler change" — it never claims first-person execution, so it is barely distinguishable from the reviewer's own proposed rewording; that near-identity is itself evidence the finding is cosmetic. Provenance is also already flagged in the e3 comment ("The thread records an actual test reverting PR 58657; the issue persisted"), and the e2 comment already declares the multi-participant fold. Substantively the blind path is correct: participant6's own conclusion in c30 was that the cause lies in the added 'module-typescript'/'commonjs-typescript' loader formats, not the .js handler change, so "do not recommend reverting PR 58657" is faithful for the reporter's case too. The only actionable residue is an optional extra clause in the e3 comment naming the maintainer/tsx-branch origin — not worth a finding.

gh_ollama_ollama_10433.summary: The case is a long evidence-gathering thread: retained `ollama runner` children under a live `ollama serve` while `ollama ps` is empty, narrowed across four Ollama releases to a scheduler race during very early runner startup (c42), fixed in v0.7.1 (c55) and verified by the reporter (c56, c57). The graph's spine is faithful — clarification chain order, the version-test-as-measurement modelling, root cause, and the verification requirement all match the thread, and images are hooked to the right turns. The main defect is that the solution hard-requires `leaked_runner_occurs_during_very_early_startup`, an id the graph itself declares engineer-inferred and that no clarification ever grants, so a correct agent can be scored down for information it cannot obtain. Secondary issues: a release-number gate in required_elements, two user answers that speak in the maintainer's voice, and no blind edge for the thread's one explicitly falsified hypothesis.
gh_ollama_ollama_10433.strengths: Measurement-class handling is exemplary and is the hardest thing to get right in this thread: the 0.6.7 (c25-c27), 0.6.8 (c33-c39), 0.7.0 (c45-c47) and debug-capture (c49-c53) round trips are all modelled as clarification_only edges with system_state_id held at S1, with the state change reserved for the actual 0.7.1 fix — and the e4 comment explicitly notes that the 0.6.7 test falsifies the "scheduler startup change already fixed it" hypothesis. The root cause matches c42 verbatim in substance (concurrent requests with varying context sizes causing frequent reloads plus clients aborting before load completes), and satisfaction_conditions correctly bar the three wrong answers the thread actually rejected (gemma3 classical leak per c19, intentional keep_alive per c14/c23, crash-orphaned runners per c8/c9). Terminal semantics separate "looks good after ~2 days" (c56) from the later "haven't seen the problem since" confirmation (c57) and require reporter verification before closing. All seven images are hooked to the right turns (img1→c6 qwen2.5-coder, img2/img3→c8, img4→c9, img5→c24 detector, img6→c27 0.6.7 test, img0→opening). The Task body is a clean opening report with no downstream knowledge, the persona_hint matches a reporter who writes bash/python diagnostics and compares PIDs, and participant2's gemma3-in-Docker report is correctly kept out of the single user side, consistent with c5 ("Your problem looks different to the OP, open a new ticket").

confirmed_findings.verifier_reasoning: Independently confirmed by enumeration over the graph: the 13 clarification info_ids are [debug_logs_capture_exact_retained_runner_pids, detector_confirms_runner_count_exceeds_active_model_count, expired_event_positive_refcount_repeats_over_one_million_times, logs_show_health_check_then_overlapping_load_and_unload, multiple_model_families_show_same_behavior, nginx_reverse_proxy_and_preloaded_models_in_use, no_clients_intentionally_set_keep_alive, ollama_067_still_leaves_extra_runner, ollama_068_reproduces_with_offending_pid_absent_from_scheduler_log, ollama_070_still_leaves_untracked_runners, problem_associated_with_vscode_continue_workload, runner_processes_remain_but_are_absent_from_ollama_ps, simple_python_api_script_does_not_reproduce] — 'leaked_runner_occurs_during_very_early_startup' is not among them; N0.info_state is the 3 opening ids; volunteered_info anywhere is only the 3 N0 ids plus N_terminal's ollama_071_verified_no_recurrence. The id appears only inside node info_states N5/N6/N7/N_terminal and in required_info.L2 + info_inferred_by_engineer. The thread confirms provenance is maintainer deduction: c38 (reporter) is only detector output + the archive + 'See the attached logs', and c39 (participant3) is the first and only statement that the offending PID's absence 'indicates the leak is during the very early startup of the runner'. This is verbatim the repo's own checklist item in scripts/make_review_docs.py: 'Engineer-only inference belongs in info_inferred_by_engineer / inference_hint, not in hard required_info.' I downgrade the reviewer's 'high' to medium for two reasons: (a) the graph does declare it in info_inferred_by_engineer, so the intent is visible and the fix is a one-line deletion; (b) mechanically the harm is muted — responder.compute_solution_call builds grounding from node_before.info_state | gathered_info_ids, and the id sits in N7.info_state, so required_info_satisfied does not actually fail an agent that reaches N7. It is a genuine contract violation and self-contradiction, not a scoring catastrophe.

confirmed_findings.claim: [logistics_gate / medium] at graph.edges[e8_N7__N_terminal].solution.required_elements_for_full_match -> "names_ollama_071_as_fixed_release" (also solution.intent "release the fix in Ollama 0.7.1" and approach_keywords "ollama_071"): Full match is gated on naming a specific future release number, which is packaging/release-schedule knowledge from the maintainer's roadmap rather than part of the diagnostic-to-fix chain.

In the thread the version number is produced purely by release scheduling: c43 reporter 'when you will release the fix?', c44 participant3 'the next release should be out within a few days', c54 reporter 'will the fix be a part of v0.7.1 or v0.7.2?', c55 participant3 'The fix will be in v0.7.1'. Nothing technical in the thread determines 0.7.1 — indeed c25/c33/c42 show the maintainer's own version predictions failing twice (0.6.7 and 0.7.0 did not fix it), so the number is unguessable from evidence by construction. scripts/make_review_docs.py states the defect class explicitly: 'No logistics gates — required_elements_for_full_match encode the technical diagnostic->fix chain, not release/packaging/scheduling remarks the engineer merely mentioned.' The gate is doubled in satisfaction_conditions item 5 ('identify Ollama 0.7.1 as the fixed release'), so an otherwise perfect answer can never reach full match. In the thread, that content is exclusively c52 (participant3): 'Yes, the PIDs are in there - go ahead and remove debug logging while I analyze the log.' The reporter's own turn c51 says only 'next try. Tell me then if it's ok, cause I will disable OLLAMA_DEBUG' followed by the detector output (3 runners / 1 active model on 0.7.0). So the simulated user would be voicing the handler's not-yet-given reply — a future-knowledge reveal, squarely the catalog's 'Coherent reveals ... stays in the user's voice (no future knowledge)' item. Unlike finding 3, this is not an observable the user can measure; it is the other party's turn. Impact is small: it leaks only a procedural acknowledgement, not diagnostic content, and the load-bearing part of the same answer (3 runners for 1 model, PIDs present in the overlapping debug logs) is faithful to c51. refuted_claims.claim: [unfaithful_reveal / medium] at graph.edges[e5_N4__N5].clarifications[0].user_answer_in_this_oncall: The user answer has the reporter state that "The offending older PID did not appear in the scheduler log at all" — a determination made by the maintainer after analysing the uploaded log, not something the reporter said or checked.
refuted_claims.why_refuted: The factual premise is right (the sentence traces to c39, participant3, not to c38), but the conclusion that this is a defect does not follow under the contract. The edge's own question_patterns include 'Does the retained runner PID appear in the 0.6.8 scheduler logs?' — that is a handler-initiated, user-executable measurement (grep the journal for a PID) and under the MEASUREMENT-CLASS rule the user_answer must 'state what the measurement showed'. What the answer states is a raw observable (a PID string is or is not present in a log the reporter owns and captured), not a diagnosis, cause, or recommendation. The persona is an admin who writes bash detectors, versions his script v8/v13, and in c40 reasons explicitly about his own log-capture window ('log_start_epoch=$((proc_start_epoch - 1800)) and the logs starts at 08:31:55') — he is plainly capable of that grep. Critically, the graph does NOT put the maintainer's inference in the user's mouth: 'leak occurs during very early startup' is deliberately kept out of the answer and parked in info_inferred_by_engineer with the e5 comment 'From the missing PID, the engineer infers...'. So the narrowing conclusion is still the agent's to draw. Under the single-simulated-user fold, the user is the only party who can answer questions about attached logs; requiring otherwise would make attached-log evidence unreachable in every graph. Legitimate encoding.

refuted_claims.claim: [graph_shape / medium] at graph.edges (no edge has solution.is_known_blind_path=true): The thread's one clearly falsified explanation — the initial brush-off that the runners are orphans from a killed/crashed server — is not modelled as a blind path anywhere, so an agent that proposes it walks a scored-neutral path instead of a penalised dead end.
refuted_claims.why_refuted: The quotes are accurate (c0 participant1 'most likely explanation is that the server was killed or crashed, orphaning the runners'; c8/c9 ps output with ppid 2268027 = the live /usr/local/bin/ollama serve; c15 the load/unload re-explanation; c17/c19 the gemma3 red herring), but c0 is a hypothesis plus a request for logs — no system-changing action was ever proposed or taken, so there is no attempt that was 'tried and did not resolve' and no post-attempt system state for an aftermath node to describe. Encoding it as a solution_only edge would mislabel a non-action as a solution, and its 'aftermath' symptoms would be identical to what e1 already collects. The refutation is in fact encoded twice already: e1's clarification runner_processes_remain_but_are_absent_from_ollama_ps has the user_answer 'The service is running and the process listing shows child ollama runner processes' (i.e. children of a live server — exactly the ps evidence that kills the orphan theory, and N1.symptoms_visible repeats it), and satisfaction_conditions item 3 explicitly prohibits 'merely an orphan caused by the main server being killed; the retained runners are observed beneath a live ollama serve process' as well as the gemma3 leak. The repo's defect catalog frames the blind-path item as a false-positive guard ('No invented failures; no ACCEPTED fix mislabeled as a blind path') and nowhere requires exhaustive blind-path coverage. Adding the edge is a defensible enrichment, not a correctness fix.

refuted_claims.claim: [future_knowledge_leak / low] at title: The task title ("Ollama 0.6.6 leaves runner processes and VRAM allocated after models disappear from ollama ps") states the runner-process finding, which is knowledge acquired later in the thread, not part of the opening report.
refuted_claims.why_refuted: The observation about provenance is correct (upstream title is 'Ollama 0.6.6 memory leak with different models'; 'runner processes' is first named by participant1 in c0 and demonstrated by the reporter in c8/c9), but it does not constitute a leak under this contract. gh_ollama_ollama_6756.summary: The case tests whether an agent resists the "your model just doesn't fit in 24 GB VRAM" reading and instead isolates an Ollama regression between 0.3.6 and 0.3.7 on AMD/ROCm, after two workarounds (OLLAMA_GPU_OVERHEAD and swapping to the official bundled-ROCm build) are falsified. The evidence chain (logs, ROCm package list, parallel-load finding, 0.3.6 downgrade at 100% GPU, official-build retest, 0.3.6-vs-0.3.7 confirmation, 0.3.14-rc0 verification) is faithfully transcribed and both blind paths are genuinely falsified in the thread — no blind_path_mislabeled. The graph fails on two scoring-relevant points: it hardens the maintainer's explicit *suspicion* about commit 0b03b9c into a required root cause, and it inverts the fix/verification order so the terminal solution is only reachable after the user has already verified the fix.
gh_ollama_ollama_6756.strengths: Both blind paths are genuinely falsified in the thread and are labeled correctly — OLLAMA_GPU_OVERHEAD (c9 at 1 GiB, c12 up to 10 GB, still segfaulting) and the official bundled-ROCm build (c22 request, c34 "the same error is still reproducible") — with aftermath nodes whose symptoms accurately describe the post-attempt state, and satisfaction_conditions[2] explicitly forbids presenting either as the resolution. The clarification answers are close paraphrases of the real replies: e1's no-custom-parameters + log narrative matches c3, the ROCm 6.0.2 package list and 32 GB RAM match c4, the parallel-load finding in e3 matches c18 nearly verbatim, and the downgrade answer reproduces c20's "21 GB / 100% GPU" ollama ps output. The multi-user folds are declared in edge comments on both e3 and e5, which is exactly right for the c44 (participant9) confirmation that the reporter himself never performed (c37: "I didn't test v0.3.7"). The Task body is clean opening-report voice with no downstream knowledge, and the persona_hint matches the reporter's observed behavior including asking for docs on the env vars (c6).

confirmed_findings.claim: The graph requires the agent to attribute the regression to the reintroduced AMD compile-flag commit and calls it something 'the maintainer isolated', but the thread only ever floats that commit as an unverified guess and never states what actually fixed 0.3.14.
confirmed_findings.verifier_reasoning: Confirmed against the source. c43 is explicitly hedged twice ('it MAY be this commit', 'MAYBE we need to back that out') and ends in a question ('Does anyone have confirmation the regression was in v0.3.7?'). c44 confirms only the version boundary ('ollama 3.6 works, 3.7 segfaults'), not the commit. c46 (same maintainer, later) still says 'There might be multiple issues lurking in here... I haven't managed to reproduce so far.' c53 announces the 0.3.14 fix with no commit and no reference back to the compile flag; c52 only says 'solved in the main branch'. Nothing in the thread ever isolates the compile-flag commit. The graph is internally inconsistent on this point too: the info_id is named suspect_reintroduced_amd_compile_flag_commit and it is correctly parked in e7.solution.info_inferred_by_engineer, yet satisfaction_conditions[0] promotes it to 'the AMD compile-configuration change the maintainer isolated' and required_elements_for_full_match[1] makes 'connects_fix_to_the_compile_configuration_change' a HARD element of full match. An agent that reports exactly what the evidence supports (0.3.6->0.3.7 AMD regression, fixed in the 0.3.14 line) is penalized for not asserting an unverified hypothesis. Not high, though: the hypothesis is the thread's own best candidate and the graph does hedge it in the id name and the inferred-by-engineer slot, so the damage is over-hardening a hedge, not encoding a wrong cause.

confirmed_findings.claim: The fix is proposed only AFTER the user has already installed and verified it: e6 makes 'test 0.3.14-rc0 containing the fix' a clarification the agent must ask before e7, and e7's own required_info includes reporter_verified_0_3_14_rc0_works.
confirmed_findings.verifier_reasoning: The circularity is real and verifiable in the graph: e7 is the solution that proposes the 0.3.14 fix, and its required_info.L3 lists reporter_verified_0_3_14_rc0_works, whose only gettable source is e6 -- the edge immediately upstream. The proposal's precondition is its own outcome. Thread order is the reverse of the graph's: c53 (maintainer) announces the fix first, c56 (reporter) verifies afterwards, and there is NO assistant turn after c56, so e7 corresponds to no real handler turn. The N6.user_perceives_resolved=false point also holds -- N6's own symptoms_visible says the reporter loads the previously failing model successfully and c56 is 'Ollama 0.3.14-rc0 works great! Thanks', which is the reporter declaring it fixed. A supporting inconsistency the reviewer missed: N6 stays on system_state_id S1 even though installing 0.3.14-rc0 is a genuine system change, while N_terminal flips to S2 on an edge that changes nothing about the user's machine. I do not sustain 'high': e6's question pattern ('Can you test the 0.3.14 release candidate containing the fix?') would plausibly absorb an agent that proposes upgrading to 0.3.14 at N5, so the correct move is not left without any edge -- it is mis-typed, not unreachable. Scoring impact is real but bounded.

pg_bug_19449.strengths: Blind-path handling is exactly right and this is the historically dominant failure mode: work_mem=128MB, disabling parallel query, and enable_memoize=0 all "worked" in the thread but were workarounds/probes, and the graph correctly models all three as clarification measurements (e1, e3) rather than solutions or dead ends, with satisfaction_conditions[3] explicitly forbidding presenting them as the fix — matching Andres's c0 framing ("Not because that should be necessary to avoid regressions, but because it will be useful to narrow down") and c4's "bumping up work_mem (to 64MB) solved this with the sample data". No fabricated blind edges were invented for c6's untried suggestions (flip joins to inner, join_collapse_limit=1 on PG15); instead e4's comment correctly records Tom Lane's c7 warning that minimizing first avoids "going down blind alleys". The clarification chain order matches the thread exactly (c0-c1 work_mem/memoize → c2-c3 dataset refresh → c4-c5 parallel + temp files + batches → c6-c8 bisect/minimize/null keys → c9-c10 fix verification), the multi-participant fold is declared in e3's comment, and every required_info id is granted by a clarification or the start info_state. Numbers are quoted accurately (2,078,995 temp files / 70GB, 63GB fileset, 262144 batches, 1.4s vs 156-161s, 3.5-4s non-parallel, commit 11c2d6fdf5af vs 1811f1af98). symptoms_visible stay observational throughout, the root cause matches c9's "prevent the 'stop-partitioning-it's-not-working' logic from triggering" reading, and the Task body contains no knowledge past the opening report.

confirmed_findings.claim: The user answer turns the IS NOT NULL observation into confirmation of the root cause ('consistent with the fix targeting null join keys'), whereas the thread states the same observation as a reason for doubt about whether the variants fail for the same reason.
confirmed_findings.verifier_reasoning: Confirmed against the source, though narrower than framed. c10 (participant3): 'Possibly. With the original (simplified) query, I get no failures with current master. And it starts failing after I revert 1811f1af98. With the alternative queries (with IS NOT NULL), it seems to work OK even after the revert. So maybe the queries are not failing for the same reason?' — and c9 (participant5) is only 'Did this commit help?'. The graph's user_answer_in_this_oncall on e5's reverting_commit_1811f1af98_restores_failure ends '...The IS NOT NULL alternatives continue to work, consistent with the fix targeting null join keys.' The two load-bearing observations (master passes; revert restores the failure; IS NOT NULL variants unaffected) are reported faithfully — only the trailing gloss is added, and it replaces the reporter's explicit doubt with an endorsement. Under the contract, user_answer states what the measurement showed; the causal reading belongs in info_inferred_by_engineer, where root_cause_parallel_hash_repartitioning_of_null_join_keys already sits. I downgrade severity to low rather than medium because (a) the gloss is not factually wrong — 1811f1af98 is literally 'Improve hash join's handling of tuples with null join keys', so a null-free variant being unaffected is genuinely consistent with it — and (b) it leaks little that the agent does not already hold: the same edge's question_patterns already name 'the null-join-key hash join change', and null-key dependence is already an established info_id from e4 (null_join_keys_are_required_for_minimal_failure, sourced from c8). The fix is a one-line rewording to preserve the hedge.

confirmed_findings.location: persona_hint.experience_level (relative to edges e3_N2__N3, e4_N3__N4, e5_N4__N5)
confirmed_findings.claim: The persona describes only an application maintainer who runs containers, changes settings and reads EXPLAIN plans, but the merged user side is required to patch and rebuild PostgreSQL, git-bisect the server, and revert a specific commit.
confirmed_findings.thread_evidence: c5 (participant3): "If I add an elog(WARNING) into ExecParallelHashJoinSetUpBatches, I see this: ... initializing 262144 batches"; c8: "I did a bit of bisecting today (with the full query), and unsurprisingly it started failing at: commit 11c2d6fdf5af..."; c10: "it starts failing after I revert 1811f1af98". These are participant3 (a PostgreSQL developer), folded into the same simulated user by the declared merge in e3's comment.
confirmed_findings.suggested_fix: Extend experience_level to state that the merged user side includes PostgreSQL core developers who can build from source, instrument executor code, run git bisect and revert commits — otherwise the user-sim may refuse or hedge the e4/e5 measurements.
confirmed_findings.verifier_reasoning: Confirmed. persona_hint.experience_level enumerates capability up to 'create large synthetic reproducers, compare server versions in containers, change PostgreSQL settings, and interpret or share EXPLAIN ANALYZE plans' — container operation and GUC changes, i.e. exactly the reporter's (participant2) ceiling as shown in c1/c3. But the merged user side must deliver core-developer work: c5 'If I add an elog(WARNING) into ExecParallelHashJoinSetUpBatches, I see this: ... initializing 262144 batches' (feeds e3.parallel_hash_join_expands_to_262144_batches), c8 'I did a bit of bisecting today (with the full query), and unsurprisingly it started failing at: commit 11c2d6fdf5af...' plus the cost-GUC-forced minimal LEFT JOIN (feeds both e4 info_ids), and c10 'it starts failing after I revert 1811f1af98' (feeds e5). The merge itself is legitimate and properly declared in e3's comment ('the reporter and reproducing PostgreSQL developers are folded into one simulated user side'), so the defect is not the merge — it is that the persona was written from the reporter alone and was not updated to cover the folded-in developers. Risk is real but bounded: user_answer_in_this_oncall is supplied verbatim for every one of these clarifications, so a sim that follows the answers will still deliver them; the exposure is hedging/refusal on the question turn, plus stylistic incoherence. Hence low, not medium.

refuted_claims.claim: Backporting to supported branches is encoded as a graded required element and satisfaction condition, but it is release/process logistics that the thread raises only as an unanswered question, so a technically correct agent is penalized on an axis the source never resolves.
refuted_claims.why_refuted: The thread quote is accurate — c11 (participant2/reporter, 2026-05-19, last message, == closed_at) asks 'when this gets fixed, will the fix only go into the latest master version, or also get backported to other still-supported versions?' and nothing follows. But that cuts against the finding rather than for it. The task graph is an ANSWER KEY, not a transcript: the reporter's final, unanswered question is precisely the thing a complete handler answer must address, and the case terminates on it. Requiring the answer to 'call for applicable backport to affected supported branches' is answering the user, not importing an external release-process axis. The encoding is also deliberately hedged rather than demanding a fact the thread lacks: satisfaction_conditions[4] says the answer must 'address applying or backporting the applicable fix to affected supported branches WITHOUT promising availability before the relevant branch builds or minor releases contain it', and e6's comment repeats 'not as an unsupported promise about an unverified package'. So the graded element demands a posture (bug fix belongs in the supported branches, don't promise a date), not an unknowable release decision. There is also no gettability problem — this is a required_element, not a required_info, so no info the user cannot supply is being demanded. The reporter's backport question is likewise already reflected in persona_hint.communication_style ('asks practical questions about backports to supported releases'), i.e. it is a deliberate, coherent modeling choice across the graph, not an accident.

refuted_claims.claim: user_perceives_resolved=true, but the reporter never observes resolution on their own system; the thread's last word from the reporter is an open question implying the fix is not yet available to them.
refuted_claims.why_refuted: The quotes are accurate but the conclusion does not follow under the declared merge. e3's comment folds the reproducing PostgreSQL developers into ONE simulated user side, which is the contract-sanctioned handling for multi-user threads. On that single merged user side, resolution IS observed first-hand in c10: 'With the original (simplified) query, I get no failures with current master. And it starts failing after I revert 1811f1af98' — a pass-with/fail-without test, i.e. stronger verification than a bare 'it works now'. N_terminal's symptoms_visible reports exactly that observable ('On a build containing the null-join-key hash join fix, the reported query completes without the runaway batch and temporary-file explosion') with no diagnosis smuggled in, and the state transition is modeled correctly: e5 is a measurement (knowledge only, so S1 is retained through N5) while N_terminal advances to S2 for the world in which the fix is actually in place. Treating c11 as evidence of non-resolution conflates 'which branches will ship it' with 'is it fixed' — c11 asks about distribution, and presupposes the fix exists ('when this gets fixed'). Note also that the reviewer's own preferred remedy is cosmetic (add a note to the terminal comment), which is a tell that the encoding is not actually wrong; and satisfaction_conditions[5] already carries the verification demand explicitly, citing the in-thread pass-with-commit/fail-after-revert test.

pg_bug_19490.summary: The case tests whether an agent can drive a cross-minor PostgreSQL streaming-replication replay stall (16.8 primary, 16.14 standby) from raw symptoms to the real root cause — a self-deadlock in RecordNewMultiXact()'s back-branch compatibility path added by 77dff5d937b1 — and land on the accepted fix (acquire MultiXactOffsetSLRULock later, as v17+ does) instead of the two falsified moves (pin 16.12, or simply delete the SimpleLruWriteAll flush). The diagnostic chain, the evidence, and the root cause are faithful to the thread. The dominant problem is structural: the start node's only outgoing edge is the known-blind-path 16.12 downgrade, so the canonical path cannot be reached without first taking a dead end that the graph's own satisfaction_conditions prohibit, while the thread's actual first handler turn was the backtrace/WAL-dump request. Three fidelity leaks compound this: engineer analysis placed in the reporter's WAL-dump answer, post-commit "all five branches pass" knowledge sitting on the pre-fix node N4, and an "initially" hedge in the opening report that telegraphs the workaround's later failure.
pg_bug_19490.strengths: The technical spine is accurate and well grounded. The root cause in e3/e5 and satisfaction_conditions matches the thread exactly: the 77dff5d937b1 back-branch compatibility path calls SimpleLruWriteAll() while RecordNewMultiXact() already holds MultiXactOffsetSLRULock (participant3, c3/c6), and the accepted fix is Andrey's "acquire it later, as it is done in 17+ branches" (c9/c11), confirmed by Heikki in c12 and applied to v14-v16 in c16 — not the tempting-but-rejected "just delete the SimpleLruWriteAll()" v1 patch, which satisfaction_conditions[3] correctly forbids with Michael Paquier's exact out-of-order ZERO_PAGE:2048 -> CREATE_ID:2047 argument from c7. Measurement class is handled correctly: the handler-requested patch trial and the cross-version replay runs (c13, c15) are modeled as clarification_only, not as solutions, and their results appear as user answers rather than as free start-state facts. The multi-user merge (participant2's backtrace, participant7's patch test, participant1's buildfarm runs folded into one user side) is explicitly declared in the e2 and e4 comments. All required_info ids are gettable (each is either in N0's info_state or granted by an e2/e4 clarification). Notably, the graph resists the logistics trap at the end of the thread: the out-of-cycle-release debate (c21-c25) and the reporter's release-notes request are correctly left out of required_elements_for_full_match, which stay purely technical.

confirmed_findings.claim: The start node's ONLY outgoing edge is the known-blind-path edge (downgrade/pin the standby to 16.12), so the canonical path to the terminal can only be reached by first taking the scored dead end — and that dead end is exactly what satisfaction_conditions forbid.
confirmed_findings.thread_evidence: The thread's actual first handler turn is not a downgrade proposal: c0 (participant1) responds to the report with the diagnostic request — "Can you get a backtrace of hanging startup process with debug symbols? Or obtain last replayed LSN and do a WAL dump in the area of deadlocked startup." — and c1 supplies the backtrace immediately, before any 16.12 aftermath is reported (that comes later, in c4). Meanwhile satisfaction_conditions[2] of the graph says "Must not present restarting or pinning the standby to 16.12 as a resolution". Also note the reporter had already performed the 16.12 downgrade himself before opening the report (body: "Downgrading the standby binary to 16.12 ... restored normal replay"), so it was never an assistant-proposed step.
confirmed_findings.suggested_fix: Add a clarification_only edge N0 -> N2 carrying the two e2 clarifications (debug backtrace, last-replayed-LSN / WAL dump), matching c0->c1/c5, and keep e1_N0__N1_x plus e2_N1_x__N2 as the optional blind branch that rejoins at N2. That way an agent that goes straight for the evidence can advance, and one that proposes pinning 16.12 lands on the aftermath node.
confirmed_findings.verifier_reasoning: Independently confirmed against the graph: the edges array has exactly one edge with from=N0, e1_N0__N1_x, edge_type solution_only, solution.is_known_blind_path=true, and every other edge chains N1_x->N2->N3->N4->N_terminal. There is no alternative exit from the start node, so the only route to the terminal runs through the blind path, while satisfaction_conditions[2] says 'Must not present restarting or pinning the standby to 16.12 as a resolution'. The thread corroborates that the first handler turn was diagnostic, not a downgrade proposal: c0 (participant1) asks 'Can you get a backtrace of hanging startup process with debug symbols? Or obtain last replayed LSN and do a WAL dump in the area of deadlocked startup', and c1 supplies a full backtrace immediately; the 16.12 failure aftermath only appears in c4. The reporter had also already performed the downgrade himself before opening the report (body Workarounds: 'Downgrading the standby binary to 16.12 ... restored normal replay'), so pinning 16.12 was never a handler-proposed step in the source. A falsified attempt IS legitimately encoded as a blind path, so the blind edge itself is fine; the defect is that it is the sole exit from N0. High severity: it makes the answer key self-contradictory and forces a scored dead end on every run.

confirmed_findings.claim: The user's answer to the WAL-dump request hands back the engineer's analysis (79871 ... is the last MultiXact on its offsets page, so the record enters the next-page compatibility path) instead of the raw dump the reporter actually produced; that inference is the crux the agent is supposed to derive at edge e3.
confirmed_findings.verifier_reasoning: Verified in both directions. c5 is posted by participant4 (the reporter — c4 and the body are both signed 'Radim') and is purely raw material: 'Altough the culprit is known, I've got more data as requested' followed by the gdb stack and the pg_waldump excerpt 'rmgr: MultiXact ... desc: CREATE_ID 79871 offset 218449 nmembers 2' surrounded by Btree INSERT_LEAF and Heap LOCK records. No page-boundary interpretation appears there. The interpretation is made by a developer, participant3, one message later in c6: '79871 is the last multixact on its offsets page, so replaying that record enters the next_pageno != pageno compatibility path added by 77dff5d937b.' The graph's e2 clarification user_answer_in_this_oncall puts that analysis in the user's mouth ('...as the last MultiXact on its offsets page, so the record enters the next-page compatibility path'), and N2.symptoms_visible[1] repeats it ('a MultiXact CREATE_ID at the end of an offsets page'), which violates the rule that symptoms_visible are observable phenomena in the user's words and not causal reasoning. The leak is partial rather than total — e3 still has to derive the self-deadlock, the same-lock reacquisition and the flush-preservation argument, which are correctly parked in info_inferred_by_engineer — so medium, not high.

confirmed_findings.claim: N4 — the node reached BEFORE the fix edge e5 — already states that the change was applied and that all five branches pass, which is post-commit knowledge and pre-announces the answer e5 is supposed to be scored on.
confirmed_findings.thread_evidence: At the point this measurement was reported (c13) the module only "reproduces the deadlock on 14, 15, and 16; 17 and 18 pass" — no fix was committed yet. The all-branches-green result exists only after Heikki's commit in c16 ("I have applied this to v14 - v16.") and is reported in c17: "I can confirm that all 5 branches are now passing new buildfarm test module. While 14-16 were failing it this morning." The graph itself models that commit as edge e5 into N_terminal, whose symptom duplicates the same sentence.
confirmed_findings.suggested_fix: At N4/e4 keep only the pre-commit facts: the module reproduces the deadlock on 14/15/16 while 17/18 pass, and the demo patch fixes the 16.8->16.14 and REL_16_0->REL_16_STABLE runs locally. Move "after applying the equivalent change, all five tested branches pass" exclusively to N_terminal / fix_applied_to_postgresql_14_through_16.
confirmed_findings.verifier_reasoning: Confirmed against the timeline. The measurement modeled at e4 is c13 (participant1), which reports only pre-commit facts: the buildfarm module 'reproduces the deadlock on 14, 15, and 16; 17 and 18 pass' — with 17/18 passing because they already acquire the lock later, not because anything was applied. c15 adds a local demo.diff test on a 16.8 primary / 16.14 standby. The commit happens later, in c16 ('I have applied this to v14 - v16.'), and only then does c17 say 'I can confirm that all 5 branches are now passing new buildfarm test module. While 14-16 were failing it this morning.' The graph nevertheless puts 'After applying the equivalent change, all five tested branches pass' into e4's second clarification answer and 'The automated cross-version replay test passes on all five tested branches after the change' into N4.symptoms_visible[2] — the same sentence N_terminal's symptom carries after e5. So the pre-fix node asserts the post-fix outcome of the very edge being scored. Medium: e5 still has to name the specific code motion and the branch set, but the agent is told in advance that the change works everywhere.

confirmed_findings.claim: The opening report is worded as 'Downgrading ... to 16.12 ... INITIALLY restored replay' / 'running the 16.12 binary initially allows replay to continue', pre-announcing at turn zero that the workaround will later fail.
confirmed_findings.verifier_reasoning: The textual facts check out. The reporter's opening post states the downgrade unqualified, twice: 'Downgrading the standby binary to 16.12 (same data directory) resolved the symptom under the same workload' and, under Workarounds, '...against the same data directory restored normal replay. After 60s under the same workload pg_stat_slru shows only 2 hits / 0 reads on MultiXact.' The failure of that workaround first appears in c4: 'pinning version down to 16.12 only avoids the MultiXactOffsetSLRU self-deadlock, but the standby then fails recovery after 12+ hours. FATAL: could not access status of transaction 24958976 ... pg_multixact/offsets/017C ... read too few bytes.' The graph's body and N0.symptoms_visible[2] both insert 'initially', and the info id is downgrade_to_16_12_initially_restores_replay. The hedge does carry the implicature that the fix did not hold, which is later-thread knowledge and blunts the blind path it is paired with. I downgrade the severity from the reviewer's medium to low: the reporter's own evidence window was a 60-second observation, so 'initially' is a mild and partly defensible paraphrase, it reveals no diagnosis or fix, and it changes no required_info or scoring element. It is a wording cleanup, not a structural defect.

refuted_claims.claim: N1_x is reached through a solution_only edge that swaps the standby binary (16.14 -> 16.12) — a real change to the user's system — yet it keeps N0's system_state_id S1.
refuted_claims.why_refuted: The premise that the binary swap happens on this edge is not supported by the source. The reporter had already run the downgrade before filing: the opening body lists it under 'Workarounds' as something done ('Downgrading the standby binary to 16.12 (same data directory) restored normal replay'), and the graph encodes that in N0.info_state as downgrade_to_16_12_initially_restores_replay plus N0.volunteered_info. So at N0 the standby is already on the 16.12 binary; e1 restates/keeps that pinning rather than effecting a fresh change, and c4 — the reviewer's own cited evidence — reads as elapsed time on the already-pinned binary ('pinning version down to 16.12 only avoids the MultiXactOffsetSLRU self-deadlock, but the standby then fails recovery after 12+ hours'), i.e. new knowledge, not a new world. Keeping S1 across N0->N1_x is therefore a defensible encoding, and node identity is unaffected because the info_state differs (downgrade_to_16_12_later_fails_recovery is added). Nothing in the thread lets me confirm a system mutation attributable to this edge, so per the default I refute. Note this interacts with finding 1: if e1 is re-scoped as a genuine assistant-proposed downgrade, the state-id question would need revisiting, but that is a consequence of fixing finding 1, not an independent defect.

bmo_1822845.summary: The case tests whether an agent resists the plausible "macOS permissions after an OS update" explanation, establishes a Firefox-111 regression, drives a bisection, and lands on the graphicsPort→CGContext partial revert. The graph's spine (N0 → permission blind path → regression → mozregression → try-build verification → revert) is a faithful reading of the thread, the blind path is genuinely falsified in-thread, and the two attachments are hooked to the right places. The one serious defect is that the try-build verification edge puts the developer's own root-cause analysis (c11) into the simulated user's mouth, handing the agent the exact answer the satisfaction conditions ask it to produce. Secondary issues: the final solution gates a full match on release-process elements, and the terminal node's symptoms are written in release-management voice rather than user-observable terms.
bmo_1822845.strengths: The permission blind path (e1 → N1_x) is correctly labelled and precisely grounded: c2 participant1 "Have you had a recent macOS update? You may have to grant permissions (again) in System Settings", c3 reporter "Traversed privacy options but I did not find toggle to allow Firefox application any permission I can grant", c4's jamf article link, and c5 "Article was not helpful because it does not involve 3rd party automator actions" — the aftermath node's symptoms mirror the reporter's own pushback, and satisfaction_conditions[1] correctly forbids settling there. The measurement-class rule is applied correctly twice: both the mozregression run (e3) and the target.dmg try-build verification (e4) are clarification_only edges with system_state_id held at S1. Attachments are correctly assigned: att9323506 is verified to be the "The 'google-translate-selection' service could not be used." dialog and sits on N0/opening_images, while att9323627 is verified to be the Automator flow (receive text in any application → Run JavaScript building the translate.google.com URL → Website Popup) and is attached to the workflow-composition clarification, matching c7. The Task body is a clean restatement of c0 with no later knowledge. e5.required_info is fully gettable (L1 via e2, L2 via e3, L3 via e4) and the stated root cause matches c11 and the landed patch summary exactly.

The users' actual replies to the try build (c13) are c14 reporter: "It works!" and c16 participant2: "I also confirm the updated build works." Nothing more. The graph's own e5.info_inferred_by_engineer lists this same id as engineer-inferred, contradicting its delivery as a user reveal.

confirmed_findings.verifier_reasoning: Independently verified in the source. The pasteboard mechanism appears exactly once, in c11 by participant1 (the handler), with an lldb backtrace through -[ChildView writeSelectionToPasteboard:types:] — 'This bug occurs because `-writeSelectionToPasteboard:types:` is called with only `NSStringPboardType` specified for `types`, so we need to partially restore …dfd7e060998e'. The users' entire response to the try build in c13 is c14 reporter 'It works!' and c16 participant2 'I also confirm the updated build works.' No user in the thread utters any part of that analysis. Yet graph.edges[e4_N3__N4].clarifications[0].user_answer_in_this_oncall ends with 'The developer's analysis: the service broke because -writeSelectionToPasteboard:types: was called with only NSStringPboardType, so part of the graphics-context change needs to be reverted.' — spoken by the simulated user. Two internal inconsistencies corroborate the defect rather than excuse it: (a) root_cause_writeselection_called_with_only_nsstringpboardtype is present in N4.info_state and N_terminal.info_state although no clarification on e4 carries that info_id and N4.volunteered_info is empty, so it enters the info_state only through this narration; (b) e5.info_inferred_by_engineer lists the identical id, and the e4 comment even states 'the root-cause reading (pasteboard types) is recorded as the engineer-inferred gain on N4' — the intent was engineer inference, but the text delivers it as a user reveal. Impact is on the primary answer key: satisfaction_conditions[0] demands precisely 'writeSelectionToPasteboard called with only NSStringPboardType'. confirmed_findings.claim: Two of the three full-match elements score release scheduling/packaging rather than the diagnostic-to-fix chain, so an agent that correctly diagnoses and proposes the partial revert is penalized for not reciting the 112.0b6 uplift and the 4/11 GA date.
confirmed_findings.thread_evidence: The technical resolution is complete at c11–c15 (analysis, patch attachment 9324195, try build, "It works!", autoland push 3980a04db6ed). The uplift/GA material only appears afterwards as pure release process: c20 participant4 "Approved for 112.0b6", c23 participant1 "released to the general population on 4/11 ... still being considered for a possible uplift to a dot release of Firefox 111, but this is not guaranteed", c25 participant5 "There is no 111 dot release planned before 112 go-live." — and only because the reporter asked in c22 "When fix will be GA?"
confirmed_findings.suggested_fix: Keep "mentions_partial_revert_of_regressing_change" as the required element; demote the uplift/GA items to optional or move them into the solution intent/concrete_example, and reword satisfaction_conditions[2] so the hard requirement is user verification on a provided build before landing, with the timeline as an optional courtesy.
confirmed_findings.verifier_reasoning: The reviewer's citations check out. The engineering resolution is complete by c11 (analysis) / c12 (attachment 9324195, the partial revert) / c13 (try build) / c14+c16 (user verification) / c15 (autoland 3980a04db6ed) / c19 (mozilla-central). Everything the two disputed elements score comes strictly later and is pure release process: c20 participant4 'Approved for 112.0b6', c21 the beta rev, c23 participant1 'released to the general population on 4/11 … still being considered for a possible uplift to a dot release of Firefox 111, but this is not guaranteed', c25 participant5 'There is no 111 dot release planned before 112 go-live. This will ride the trains with 112.' — and it surfaces only because the reporter asked c22 'When fix will be GA?'. Neither the 4/11 date nor the 112.0b6 target is derivable from any evidence the graph makes gettable; they are Mozilla release-train facts held by the release managers. Making them required_elements_for_full_match, and hard-coding them into satisfaction_conditions[2], grades packaging knowledge rather than the diagnosis-to-fix chain, and satisfaction_conditions[3] already carries the genuine user-verification requirement, so [2]'s verification clause is not load-bearing. Partial defense that keeps this below high: 'mentions_uplift_or_release_vehicle' is a defensible expectation for a regression in a shipped release where the reporter explicitly asks about availability — a competent handler should say the fix rides a release vehicle even without naming 112.0b6. 'gives_honest_ga_timeline' as written (specific GA date, no-promise-of-dot-release) is the clearly unfair one. Confirmed but the reviewer's medium is right, not high.

bmo_1865928.summary: The case tests a Firefox 120 regression where YUV->NV12 conversion was enabled for Release on a GPU (ATI Radeon HD 2600 XT / AMDPreUVD4) that does not support NV12, producing all-green YouTube frames; the diagnostic chain is media-playback profile -> about:support gfx flags -> mozregression window -> pref-flip confirmation -> find-fix + beta test build, resolved by backing the regressor out for 120.0.1 and by bug 1865426's NV12 support check for 121+. The graph's skeleton, root cause, measurement-class handling and blind path are all faithful to the thread. The dominant problem is voice: three of the four clarification answers put developers' analytic conclusions into the reporter's mouth, and in the mozregression answer this hands over the regressing preference name (gfx.video.convert-yuv-to-nv12.image-host-win) that in the real thread was only identified by Mozilla engineers two days and many comments later — that leak effectively pre-answers the case.
bmo_1865928.strengths: The technical skeleton is right and well grounded. (1) The single blind path e6 is genuine and correctly labeled: c56 shows participant6 tried all three of layers.iosurfaceimage.use-nv12 / media.wmf.use-nv12-format / media.wmf.zero-copy-nv12-textures with no effect, and N2_x's symptoms describe exactly that post-attempt state — no blind_path_mislabeled, no fabricated_blind_path. (2) Measurement-class discipline is correct and non-obvious here: the gfx.video.convert-yuv-to-nv12.image-host-win flip (c30/c31) is modeled as a clarification even though it doubles as a workaround, and the mozregression / find-fix / beta-test-build runs are clarifications too, with the edge comment on e3 explicitly justifying it. (3) The root cause in satisfaction_conditions and the e5 solution match c58 verbatim in substance (bug 1857385 set the pref true for Release; backed out for 120.0.1; bug 1865426's NV12 support check fixes 121+), and the requirement not to permanently disable HWA is the right shape given the reporter's own workaround. (4) The multi-user merge with participant6 is declared in both e6's comment and e4's answer text. (5) Image assignment is exact: att9364836/9364837 are the HWA-on/HWA-off screenshots from c0/c1 on N0, att9365718 is the mozregression progress shot on e2, att9365938/9365956 are the two find-fix progress shots on e4. (6) required_info is fully gettable, about_support_shows_zero_copy_and_overlay_blocked_on_old_amd is correctly demoted to info_inferred_by_engineer, and the persona_hint (first-time mozregression user, asked how to run a test build without touching the main profile — c40, c52) matches the reporter's behaviour precisely. (7) The Task body is clean of later-thread knowledge.

I'm not sure what/how to report the results here, but here goes" followed by six raw pushlog URLs. c21 (participant5) only narrows it: "From comment #20, The regression window is https://hg.mozilla.org/integration/autoland/pushloghtml?fromchange=431b4ea6&tochange=52459518". Move the pushlog->pref-enable mapping into the engineer's side (info_inferred_by_engineer / inference_hint on the e5 solution), and rename the info_id to something evidence-shaped (e.g. mozregression_window_pushlog_2023_11_07_to_11_21) so the agent must derive the regressor rather than be told it.
confirmed_findings.verifier_reasoning: Confirmed against the thread. c18 (reporter) is explicitly ignorant of what his run points at ("I'm not sure what/how to report the results here") and dumps six raw pushlog URLs; c19/c20 are just the log and progress screenshot. c21 (participant5, a triager on the Mozilla side, not a fellow user) only narrows the window to fromchange=431b4ea6&tochange=52459518 -- still pure changesets. The pref is first uttered by participant7 at c30, explained as the regressor at c39 ("That's the pref the initial regressing bug changed in Fx120") and confirmed at c58 (bug 1857385 set it true for Release). So the mapping pushlog-window -> 'the push that enabled gfx.video.convert-yuv-to-nv12.image-host-win' is upstream repo knowledge derived by Mozilla engineers, not something the reporter possessed or could read off his own artifacts. I considered two defenses and both fail: (a) the multi-user merge -- the one user who does name the pref in his own voice is participant6 at c56, i.e. after c30, so placing it at e2 still moves knowledge backwards in time; (b) the measurement-class rule ("user_answer states what the measurement showed") -- what mozregression showed is a changeset range, not the semantics of the push. This is materially different from findings 2/3, where the content sits inside an artifact the user physically holds and can read out. Impact is real: the pref name is the answer key's central term (root cause condition, e3's confirmation question, e6's blind-path contrast), and handing it at turn 2 of 5 collapses the diagnostic work to mechanical confirmation. The proposed fix (evidence-shaped info_id, mapping moved to info_inferred_by_engineer / inference_hint on e5) is the right shape.

bmo_1913022.summary: The case tests whether an agent can resist two dismissal-style resolutions (close-as-duplicate, "install a third-party extension") and instead localize the regression to the IDN rework that intentionally deleted the network.IDN_show_punycode code path, then restore an opt-in punycode display covering desktop and Android with post-landing verification. Structurally the graph is a faithful and well-built rendering of the thread: both blind paths are genuinely falsified, the bisection is correctly a clarification edge, and the root cause matches bug 1889536/1911935. Two defects would corrupt scoring: the bisection clarification's user_answer hands the agent the root-cause conclusion that the graph elsewhere declares must be engineer-inferred, and the terminal node carries the reporter's "still not fixed" recording as if it were proof of resolution. Several symptom fields also carry analysis rather than observations.
bmo_1913022.strengths: Blind-path labelling is correct on both attempts, which is the historically dominant failure mode and it is clean here: e1 (close as duplicate of bug 1332714, c4/c9) was rejected with evidence by the reporter (c7/c8: "the bug has been flagged as resolved but is not") and disputed by a contributor (c6), and e3 (recommend the punycode-domain-detection add-on, c13) was falsified at c15 ("This extension doesn't work... works only for few domains") and on Android at c2, after which participant4 reopened the bug (c16). The winning path (restore the pref) is correctly NOT marked blind. The measurement-class rule is respected: the regression-window bisection is a clarification_only edge, not a solution. The root cause matches the thread and the bug metadata (regressed_by 1889536, see_also 1911935 cleanup) and the fix intent quotes the real mechanism from c16 ("Making isLabelSafe return early on a pref-bound atomic bool check"). Chronology is right — the duplicate closure hangs off N0 (08:53) and the extension recommendation off N2 (10:35, after the 09:12 window). The contract requires satisfaction_conditions to demand user verification before declaring resolution, and this thread's single most instructive failure mode is exactly a verification failure: c27-c29 the reporter tests Nightly 131.0a1 one hour after the landing, concludes 'The BUG looks to me to be not resolved', and attaches a gif; c30 has to correct him ('only landed 1 hr ago - updates to Nightly are twice a day AFAIK ... wait for the _next_ update'); c31 he is still confused ('The version number that I can see in the fix are the same of the version I tested'). Preempting that is diagnostic-to-resolution work, not release-process trivia, and it is publicly-knowable information present in the thread rather than a hidden internal fact. The element is also internally consistent with satisfaction_conditions[2], which already demands 'verification guidance that accounts for the Nightly update cadence (a build from before the landing cannot show the fix)', and the solution.intent frames it as verification guidance, not as a cadence recital.
